newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS - Oil makes Norway rich, inflation fears loom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil makes Norway rich, inflation fears loom.

text.p: Norway, one of the few European countries to enjoy a budget surplus, has watched its state coffers swell as a recent rally in oil prices has taken crude markets to near six-year highs.
But analysts say the feel-rich, feel-good factor could backfire and lead to stagnation in the mainland sector of the economy or to higher prices and costs.
Norway's economy has never looked better. Thanks to an abundance of natural resources, public finances began running at a surplus last year.
The Scandinavian country is the world's second largest crude exporter after OPEC giant Saudi Arabia and ranks in the top five suppliers of gas to continental Europe.
According to the government's draft budget proposal for 1997, the surplus is expected to reach 37.9 billion crowns ($5.8 billion) in 1996 and rise to 40.9 billion crowns next year.
The surplus, at least for 1996, is likely to be larger. The government's 1996 estimate was based on an oil price of 125 crowns per barrel. So far this year it has averaged 128.50.
But despite the ever-growing mountain of cash, analysts say a consistently high oil price could have a downside by tipping the delicate economic balance.
Norway's minority Labour government has proposed a restrictive budget for 1997 to keep inflation under check from increasing demand and wage growth.

Analysts say the government, facing parliamentary elections next year, is likely to come under increasing pressure from opposition parties to increase public spending, which itself would lead to higher prices.
"It may be very tempting for the opposition parties to say there are many good causes that should be paid for and we have the money to do it now," said one analyst.
"But we need a tight fiscal policy. A weaker, watered down budget will only lead to higher inflation.".
Inflationary pressure also grows as the Norwegian crown -- considered a petroleum currency -- strengthens in line with firmer oil markets.

"The crown has strengthened, keeping short-term interest rates down, which has kept bond yields down. But the rally in the debt market is somewhat based on sand," said Knut Anton Mork, chief economist at Handelsbanken.
"I see clouds on the horizon from inflation due to wage growth and higher domestic consumption. The appreciation of the crown may overstimulate the economy."
Harald Magnus Andreassen, chief economist at Elcon Securities, says a stronger currency also threatens competitiveness of mainland industry.

"My worry is that we will feel too rich and behave like it. High oil prices could lead to stagnation of mainland industry and to the economy as a whole. The consequences are in 10 or 20 years from now, that's the problem."

The central bank has come under increasing pressure to stem the crown's rise. This has meant increasing intervention on foreign exchange markets, given the bank's reluctance to trim interest rates and risk triggering inflation.

Leif Eide, director of the bank's market operations department, says its selling of crowns is partly to maintain a stable exchange rate and partly to cover investments for the government petroleum fund, in which the budget surplus is invested.
So far this year the bank has sold about 52 billion crowns on the foreign exchange market against an expected 37.9 billion crown budget surplus.

"Part of the intervention is to cover investments for the petroleum fund but the goal of our monetary policy is to stabilise the exchange rate. We have said the economy doesn't need a shot in the arm, so we are not happy to see lower interest rates," Eide said.
"In the present stage of the Norwegian economy it is accepted that that central bank buys more (foreign currency) than is needed for the petroleum fund."

Eide estimates that at current oil prices of around $25 per barrel, or 160 crowns, the bank will have to buy foreign currency for between 50 and 52 billion crowns to meet investments in the fund in 1996. ($1=6.537 Norwegian Crown)
